column9: HMS Alert and HMS Discovery lying under the perpendicular wall of Sanderson's Hope, a thousand feet of rock north of Upernavik cleft by a narrow fiord, with a small berg between them. Moss records that the ships stopped for an hour a mile or two on to shoot enough looms for two dinners of fresh food for all hands, and that they groped through fog next day into Upernavik harbour.

A young Greenlander in sealskin standing on the shore holding up a string of fish. Moss drew him on the outward voyage, on the coast where the expedition completed its stock of dogs at Proven and took on Hans Hendrik as dog driver for HMS Discovery. Position is Proven, where the ships called; the boy is not named in the book.

Two of the expedition standing beside a splendid erratic block of red granite twelve or fifteen feet high in Twin Glacier Valley, Hayes Sound, with the twin glaciers behind. Moss records that a complete trench was worn deep into the ground round the block by the footprints of musk oxen rubbing against it, that every boulder large enough had been used as a scratching post, and that at the upper end of the valley the party found the remains of Inuit houses with door posts made of whale ribs.

Three walrus lying on the edge of a floe, drawn by Moss beside his account of the hunt from a whale-boat with a harpoon gun in her bows near Franklin Pierce Bay. He records the animal measuring twelve and a half feet from nose to tail and eleven and a half in girth, its tusks eighteen inches from gum to point, used to dig up the molluscs it fed on and to hook itself up onto the floes; the meat went to the dogs, who had been living almost entirely on preserved Australian meat and disliked dog biscuit, and walrus liver figured on the officers' breakfast table for some days.
